slot.brief: Set of statements on why nitrogen differs from heavier group-15 elements (no d-orbitals, small size, N2 triple bond, lack of catenation); ask which combination of statements is valid.

stem:
Consider the following statements about the anomalous behaviour of nitrogen:
I. Nitrogen does not form pentahalides because its valence shell has no vacant $d$ orbitals.
II. Its small size permits effective $p\pi$–$p\pi$ overlap and favors multiple bonding.
III. Nitrogen cannot show positive oxidation states in compounds because it is more electronegative than most elements.
IV. The strong triple bond in $\text{N}_2$ contributes to the existence of elemental nitrogen mainly as diatomic molecules.
V. The $\text{N}-\text{N}$ single bond is weaker than the $\text{P}-\text{P}$ bond due to greater lone-pair repulsion, so nitrogen shows less catenation.
Which combination of statements is valid?
options: II, III, IV and V only
I, II, IV and V only

verdicts.working: I, II, IV and V are valid in the standard BITSAT treatment. III is false: nitrogen has positive oxidation states in compounds such as NO₂ and N₂O₅.

working:
I, II, IV and V are valid.
III is false: nitrogen can have positive oxidation states in compounds with more electronegative elements such as oxygen and fluorine.

Independent check: I, II, IV and V are valid in the standard BITSAT treatment. III is false: nitrogen has positive oxidation states in compounds such as NO₂ and N₂O₅.
solution: Nitrogen lacks vacant $d$ orbitals and cannot expand its octet to form pentahalides (I). Its small size favors effective $p\pi$–$p\pi$ overlap and multiple bonding (II); the strong $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ bond makes elemental nitrogen predominantly diatomic (IV). Greater lone-pair repulsion weakens the $\text{N}-\text{N}$ single bond relative to $\text{P}-\text{P}$, reducing catenation (V). Nitrogen can show positive oxidation states, so III is false; hence (D).
